_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: He holds like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: and our question is about the Rabbis.
rashi:a2.1: It is impossible to coincide precisely: therefore they would not break the neck, since each town says: I am not the nearest.
rashi:a2.2: It is possible to coincide precisely: and “nearest” includes even [several] nearest towns.
rashi:a3.1: And stipulate: as we explained above.
rashi:a4.1: Everyone agrees it is possible to coincide precisely: they hold like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
rashi:a5.1: What conclusion was reached about it: according to the Rabbis.
rashi:a5.2: Two heifers: since it is possible to coincide precisely, and “nearest” includes even [several] nearest towns.
rashi:a6.1: Let them bring two: since they cannot make a stipulation, as the two [towns] are equal.
rashi:a6.2: It is impossible to coincide precisely: therefore they can make a stipulation.
rashi:a7.1: The healthy one came out first: out of its great vigor it went ahead of its brother.
rashi:a8.1: The priest takes the lean one: according to Rabbi Akiva.
rashi:a8.2: But didn’t we learn “they assess [meshammenin]”: which implies that whatever the one is worth more than the other, they divide that money.
rashi:a8.3: While you were eating dates [kafnayata] in Babylonia: while you were eating dates in Babylonia and pampering yourself.
rashi:a8.4: We explained it: this statement of Rabbi Akiva, and we inferred it from the latter clause.
rashi:a9.1: That they divide between them: that both have a share in both [lambs]; then here too let them divide the living one.
rashi:a9.2: The fat will be between them: whatever the one is fatter and better than the other is left lying between them, and over it they come to judgment, and the Israelite claims against the priest: Bring a proof, etc., just as Rabbi Akiva holds in the latter clause: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.
rashi:a10.1: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir: for the unattributed mishna teaches: he is obligated in the gifts.
rashi:a10.2: If it is a firstborn, all of it is mine: and the one that I took would be non-sacred, and I would return it to you and take the gifts from it.
rashi:a11.1: And he sold it to the Israelite in its blemish: and then took the other one as its replacement. And a firstborn that a priest sold to an Israelite is exempt from the gifts, since it is compared to the gazelle and the deer, in the first chapter (above, Bekhorot 12a).
rashi:a11.2: They rendered one who does not acquire like one who acquires: even though the priest did not acquire that one, since it never reached his hands, they treated it as though he had acquired it. Since from the outset the priest had a hand in it, for perhaps it is his, the Rabbis treated it as though it had reached his hands as a firstborn.
rashi:a12.1: In an uncertain firstborn whose replacement is not in the hand of the priest: who took nothing in its place, as when the mishna teaches: a male and a female, the priest has nothing here. That male is an uncertain firstborn, since perhaps the female came out first; it grazes, and is eaten in its blemish by the owners.
rashi:a12.2: That it is obligated in the gifts: for here one cannot say they treated it as if the priest had sold it to the Israelite, since nothing came into the priest’s hand as a replacement.
rashi:a14.1: If you deem him obligated: [if you deem] an uncertain firstborn obligated in the gifts, he will come to say it is entirely non-sacred, and will come to permit shearing and labor.
rashi:a15.1: And how can you say: that Rabbi Yosei’s reason is because of shearing and labor?
tosafot:a8.1: While you were eating kafnayata in Babylonia, we explained it: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: while you were eating dates in Babylonia and pampering yourself, we toiled to settle it; and Rabbeinu Shmuel explained it the same way in chapter Beit Kor (Bava Batra 107b). But this is difficult: he should have said “dates” [temarim], for kafnayata is a term of inferiority, as is said at the beginning of Bekhol Me’arvin (Eruvin 28b) that kafniyot may not be bought with second-tithe money. Rather, I say the meaning is: it would have been better for you to be with me, toiling in halakha and explaining it, than to be eating kafniyot in Babylonia.
tosafot:a11.1: They rendered one who does not acquire like one who acquires: That which is said at the end of Kol HaGet (Gittin 30a), about one who lends money to a priest or a Levite so as to separate [their gifts] for them from their share, “Whose view is this? Rabbi Yosei, who said they rendered one who does not acquire like one who acquires,” refers to the Rabbi Yosei here, since it is all one reasoning: there too his replacement is in the priest’s hand, since he gave him the money. And it does not refer to the Rabbi Yosei of chapter Shnayim Oḥazin (Bava Metzia 12a), about one who hires a laborer, [that] his son may gather [gleanings] after him, where Rabbi Yosei’s reasoning is explained as being that they rendered one who does not acquire like one who acquires. For there it is a different reason, an ordinance for the poor, as is explained there: the poor themselves are content with it, etc. And now, according to what [the Gemara there] asks, there is no difficulty in the fact that Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yosei in that case of Shnayim Oḥazin, while in Gittin [the Gemara] does not want to establish the mishna there according to Rabbi Yosei but says, “We do not establish it according to an individual opinion”: for perhaps [Shmuel] does not hold like the Rabbi Yosei of Gittin.
gershom:a1.1: He holds like Rabbi Yosei [HaGelili]. And still, according to Rava [so the printed text; the sense seems to be: according to the Rabbis], we do not know whether the first tanna holds that it is impossible to coincide precisely, so that both [towns] count as distant, as we said about the oven [17b].
gershom:a2.1: And how can you understand: for the first tanna, if it is impossible to coincide precisely, then one of them must be the nearest.
gershom:a3.1: Let them bring one heifer in partnership and stipulate: If I am the nearest, let the heifer be on my account; and if my fellow [town] is the nearest, let it be on its account.
gershom:a4.1: What conclusion was reached about it: according to the Rabbis, is it possible or impossible?
gershom:a5.1: Rather, conclude from it that [the Rabbis] hold it is impossible to coincide precisely, and that is why they bring one and stipulate, as we said.
gershom:a6.1: Rabbi Ḥiyya [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba] said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: The “they assess” that Rabbi Akiva said means that they assess which of the two is the lean one, and the priest takes only the lean one.
gershom:a7.1: Rabbi Ḥiyya [bar Abba] said to Rabbi Yoḥanan: at the time he learned this halakha from him.
gershom:a8.1: But didn’t we learn “they assess”: which implies that they divide the added value equally.
gershom:a10.1: From the latter clause: from the inference of the latter clause, “the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.” For if it should enter your mind that “they assess between them” means dividing everything equally, then in the latter clause too let them divide equally.
gershom:a11.1: Rather, what does “they assess” mean? The fat will be between them. That is, Rabbi Akiva holds that the priest has the lower hand: they assess the lean one, and the fat by which the other is better than this one is [left] between them. The Israelite says to him: Bring a proof that this one is the firstborn, and take it; and if not, you have nothing more.
gershom:a12.1: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who obligates in the gifts? [A printed gloss here: “Our master’s words are not understood, for apparently the unattributed mishna, which is Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yosei both speak within the dispute of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon, and according to all, the second grazes until it becomes blemished. This needs study.”] According to Rabbi Akiva there is no need to ask why he obligates, for since he requires it to graze and become blemished, certainly its law is that it is obligated in the gifts once it has become blemished. But according to Rabbi Meir, who does not require it to become blemished, why does he obligate it in the gifts? It still has the law of a firstborn upon it!
gershom:a13.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Since the priest comes upon him from two sides, etc. And therefore, even if it has not become blemished, he is obligated in the gifts.
gershom:a14.1: And there are books in which it is written, “What is the reasoning of Rabbi Akiva?”, and they answer in the same way according to his reasoning: since the priest comes upon him, etc.
gershom:a15.1: They rendered the one the priest does not acquire, which is in the Israelite’s hand, exempt from the gifts, like the one he does acquire, which is in the priest’s hand and is exempt. Even though he did not acquire that other one, the Rabbis treated it as though he had, and it is regarded as though he sold the Israelite a blemished firstborn in exchange for this one that the priest acquired for himself. It turns out that the replacement for the Israelite’s animal is in the priest’s hand, and he sold him everything, the body and the gifts. Therefore Rabbi Yosei exempts.
gershom:a16.1: Everyone concedes in an uncertain firstborn whose replacement is not in the hand of the priest: as in the uncertain case of a male and a female, where the priest has nothing here; that one is certainly obligated in the gifts.
gershom:a17.1: Lest you say Rabbi Yosei’s reason is not because of the replacement, but because if you obligate him in the gifts he will think it is non-sacred and come to shear it; therefore, even though there is no replacement, he should be exempt.
gershom:a18.1: It teaches us: Rabbi Elazar [teaches] that it is because of the replacement, and where there is no replacement he is obligated.
gershom:a19.1: And how can you say this: that it should enter our minds that Rabbi Yosei’s reason is that if you obligate him, he will say [it is non-sacred]?
gershom:a20.1: But doesn’t the latter clause teach: explicitly, Rabbi Yosei said: Any whose replacements, etc. Evidently his reason is because of the replacement.
rashi:b3.1: In an uncertain tithe: for example, where one of the tithed animals jumped back among them, of which we say in “chapter 2” [so the printed text; the passage is below, Bekhorot 58b] that all of them graze until they become blemished and are eaten in their blemish by the owners. An uncertain tithe: the priest does not come upon him from two sides, since if it is tithe the priest has no share in it, as tithe is sacrificed as a peace offering and eaten by the owners.
rashi:b5.1: And how can you say this: that Rabbi Meir’s reason is so that the category of the gifts should not be forgotten?
rashi:b5.2: Any whose replacements, etc.: Granted, if you say that Rabbi Meir’s reason with regard to a firstborn is that [the priest] comes upon him from two sides, that is why Rabbi Yosei took up the reasoning that since its replacement is in the priest’s hand it is exempt: [the priest] cannot say, “If it is a firstborn, it is all mine,” since it is as though he sold it to the Israelite. But if you say Rabbi Meir’s reason is so that the category of the gifts should not be forgotten, why does Rabbi Yosei give the reason that its replacements are in the priest’s hand? For according to Rabbi Meir too, on this reasoning, it should be exempt! Rather, the reason is certainly not so that the category of the gifts should not be forgotten.
rashi:b7.1: If the fat one died, it is the priest’s: this one that died, since Rabbi Tarfon said the priest chooses the better one.
rashi:b7.2: Rabbi Tarfon retracted: from his first ruling, where he said the priest chooses the better one; and he holds that both have a share in both.
rashi:b8.1: To two who deposited with a shepherd: two animals, and one of them died, and it is not known whose died.
rashi:b8.2: That the shepherd places: [it] between the two of them to divide, and withdraws; for here one cannot say “the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.” And in the mishna too, where Rabbi Tarfon says they divide, it is a case where that living uncertain firstborn was handed over to a shepherd, and the homeowner and the priest come to the shepherd; so there is no claimant taking from his fellow, since it is not in the possession of either of them.
rashi:b9.1: And Rabbi Akiva’s parable, to one who deposited with a homeowner: and he put it in his flock, and one animal in his flock died, and he says: Yours died, and the other says: One of yours died. The burden of proof rests upon the claimant. And in the mishna too, where Rabbi Akiva weakens the priest’s position, it is when they are in the homeowner’s possession, so the priest is a claimant taking from his fellow.
rashi:b10.1: Rather, about what do they disagree: since the mishna is not explained as one and the same case.
rashi:b10.2: Does Rabbi Akiva disagree about two who deposited with a shepherd: said in astonishment. There, certainly, one cannot say “the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.”
rashi:b11.1: They disagree only: for example, where the living firstborn stands in the homeowner’s courtyard, and a priest tends all of the homeowner’s animals.
rashi:b11.2: He transfers to him: the homeowner [transfers] to the priest a place in his courtyard, so that the priest acquires the firstborn animals as soon as they are born, his courtyard acquiring them for him.
rashi:b11.3: For a person is content that a mitzva be performed with his property: that the priest’s firstborn animals be raised in his courtyard. So it becomes the courtyard of both of them, and this courtyard is like the shepherd, as though two had deposited with him. Therefore they divide, since it stands in the possession of both.
rashi:b12.1: A loss: where there is an uncertainty, the homeowner loses if the courtyard stands in the priest’s possession.
tosafot:b10.1: Everyone concedes about two who deposited with a shepherd, etc.: In chapter HaMafkid (Bava Metzia 37b), [the Gemara] raises a contradiction between this statement of Rava and another statement of Rava, about what Rava said, that in the case of two bundles he should have been careful, etc.
tosafot:b10.2: That the shepherd places it between them and withdraws: This is not like the case of one who robbed one of five people, where we say he places the stolen item between them and withdraws, and [the Gemara] asks in chapter HaMafkid (ibid.): But then they will all take it and go! And didn’t Rabbi Abba bar Zavda say: An uncertain item that is left aside, one should not take ab initio, and if one took it, one need not return it? And it explains that “places,” said about the robber, means that he leaves it in his own hand or in the hand of the court until it is clarified whose it is. But here we are not concerned if they all take it and go, since it is a case where they deposited with him without his consent, and he is not obligated to guard it, and it is not an item left aside in uncertainty. And if “withdraws” here means that they divide between them, it is exactly like Rabbi Tarfon’s ruling. And if it means “withdraws, and whoever is stronger prevails,” one must say that when [the Gemara] compares Rabbi Tarfon’s case to two who deposited with a shepherd, it means this: since there, whoever is stronger prevails and we do not say “the burden of proof rests upon the claimant,” it is reasonable to institute likewise with the priest (that they divide).
tosafot:b11.1: He transfers to him a place in his courtyard: And even without a formal act of acquisition [the priest] acquires, since [the homeowner] resolves to do so and binds himself. Alternatively, the shepherd often opens and locks, as it is said, “Let her go and lock and open,” and so he takes possession in the homeowner’s property.
gershom:b1.1: Lest you say Rabbi Yosei does not require a replacement, but spoke according to Rabbi Meir’s words, etc. Therefore Rabbi Elazar had to say that he is obligated.
gershom:b2.1: In an uncertain tithe: for example, where he called the ninth “tenth,” the tenth “ninth,” and the eleventh “tenth”: all three are consecrated; the tenth is tithe, the ninth is [eaten] in its blemish [the printed text reads “sacrificed in its blemish”], and the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering. That is an uncertain tithe, which is exempt from the gifts, since [the priest] cannot come upon him from two sides. All the more so a certain tithe is exempt, since it is an offering of lesser sanctity and the Israelite eats all of it except the portions burned on the altar.
gershom:b3.1: And Rabbi Meir obligates [only there]. Evidently Rabbi Meir obligates only for a firstborn, where [the priest] comes from two sides, but for tithe he does not obligate, and Rav Pappa’s statement is not needed.
gershom:b4.1: It is still needed: lest you say Rabbi Meir, etc. Rav Pappa teaches us that it is exempt according to all.
gershom:b5.1: And why should they divide? He himself said that the priest chooses the better one, since the healthy one came out first.
gershom:b6.1: Let us see: now, if the fat one died, which is the healthy one, it is the priest’s, etc.
gershom:b7.1: Rabbi Tarfon retracted: from what he had said at first, that [the priest] chooses; rather he holds that they divide, even when both are alive.
gershom:b8.1: Rabbi Akiva says: The burden of proof rests upon the claimant, etc. That is, it stands in the homeowner’s possession, and the priest must bring a proof.
gershom:b9.1: To two who deposited two animals with a shepherd, and one of them died, and the shepherd does not know whose died: the law is that he places the living one between them and withdraws, and it is money lying in doubt, and they divide. So too the one that is alive is placed between them, between the priest and the Israelite; therefore they divide.
gershom:b10.1: To one who deposited one animal with a homeowner, and it mixed into his flock, and one of the flock died, and it is not known whether it is the homeowner’s or the depositor’s: the law there is that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.
gershom:b11.1: Rather, about what do they disagree? Since Rabbi Ḥiyya says that the words of this one and the words of that one appear [right], and brings a proof for each, about what do they disagree? Why do they not concede to each other? Are not both agreed about two who deposited with a shepherd, that such is the law, and agreed too about one who deposited with a homeowner? Does Rabbi Akiva disagree about two who deposited with a shepherd? [That is,] even though one can say that the shepherd places it between them and withdraws, does Rabbi Akiva nevertheless say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant?
gershom:b12.1: And does Rabbi Tarfon disagree about one who deposited? That is, they do not disagree; rather, everyone concedes about two and about one, etc.
gershom:b13.1: Everyone concedes about two who deposited with a shepherd: that is, if the homeowner handed his animal that had not given birth to a shepherd, so that the priest too has a claim on it, and it gave birth to two males in the shepherd’s possession, certainly the law is that they divide. And about one who deposited with a homeowner: for example, where it is in the homeowner’s possession, and the homeowner handed the animal to a priest who is a shepherd.
gershom:b14.1: Rabbi Tarfon holds: he transfers to him. The homeowner [transfers] to the priestly shepherd a place in his courtyard where his firstborn will be, for the homeowner is content that a mitzva be done in his courtyard, that the priest’s firstborn be raised there. So it is like two who deposited with a shepherd: the two are the priest and the homeowner, and the courtyard is the shepherd, since both have rights in it.
gershom:b15.1: That he places the stolen item [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf here speaks of the shepherd placing the animal] between them: therefore they divide.
gershom:b16.1: And Rabbi Akiva holds: since there is a loss to the homeowner, for sometimes the firstborn dies, and the priest comes and says: It was not the firstborn that died, but one of your animals. Because of this concern he does not transfer a place to him, and the priest at the courtyard is like one who deposited with a homeowner, and the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. [The Gemara] chose “two who deposited with a shepherd” and “one who deposited with a homeowner” because it is people’s way for two to deposit their animals with a shepherd, and for one to deposit with a homeowner.
gershom:b17.1: For the one that bore a single offspring is superior: since it had room, as no other one pressed it, and it is the certain firstborn; so one might say that even according to Rabbi Akiva the priest takes the fat one.
gershom:b18.1: In this case of two ewes that had not given birth, Rabbi Akiva says the priest takes the lean one, since neither had given birth, and we are uncertain which one bore the lean one, whether the one that bore a male and a female or the one that bore a male alone, so a proof is needed. [A printed gloss: It seems one should read: “But where one had given birth and one had not, the one that had not given birth is superior, and one might say the priest takes the healthy one; it was necessary, etc.”] For the one that had not given birth is superior, and [one might say] the priest takes the healthy one. It was necessary [to teach them all], since in all of them Rabbi Akiva disagrees.
rashi:b13.1: Mishna. One is his: since there was a female with it, one can say the female came out first.
rashi:b13.2: They assess between them: the priest takes the lean one.
rashi:b14.1: They divide: for Rabbi Tarfon retracted from his first ruling.
rashi:b14.2: Two males and two females, the priest has nothing here: for one can say that each one bore a male and a female, and the female came out first.
rashi:b16.1: Whose replacements are in the hand of the priest: since the priest takes one of the uncertain ones, the other is exempt from the gifts, since they rendered one who does not acquire like one who acquires.
rashi:b16.2: A male and a female, the priest has nothing here: for perhaps the one that had not given birth bore the female, and the one that had already given birth bore the male.
rashi:b17.1: Gemara. The first: a ewe that bore two males; there Rabbi Akiva says the priest takes the lean one.
rashi:b17.2: Because two from one: [the two] came out of one ewe, and the matter is uncertain, and the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.
rashi:b18.1: But two ewes: that bore two males and a female, where two came out of one and one from the other.
rashi:b18.2: Say he concedes to Rabbi Tarfon: that the priest chooses the better one, for it is better precisely because it came out alone and the female was not with it, and this one is certainly a full firstborn.
rashi:b18.3: And this one that bore a single one is superior: shevi’aḥ means excellent.
